title: Lewis v. State
description: Whether venue for felony murder charges, where the predicate felony occurred in one county and the death in another, should be determined by a proximate-cause analysis or by the location of the defendant's conduct.
plaintiff_argument: Lewis argued that venue was improper in Gwinnett County because the predicate felony (drug sale) occurred in DeKalb County, and the trial court erred by using a proximate-cause analysis instead of focusing on where his conduct "inflicted" the cause of death.
defendant_argument: The State argued that venue was proper in Gwinnett County because the deaths occurred there and were the natural and reasonably foreseeable result of Lewis's actions, justifying the trial court's proximate-cause analysis.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the trial court's order denying Lewis's motion to dismiss and remanded the case, ruling that the trial court erred by applying a proximate-cause framework to a venue question.

title: Guy v. Hous. Authority of Augusta
description: Whether a local housing authority is protected from a personal injury suit by sovereign immunity as an instrumentality of a municipality, requiring an analysis of common law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that the housing authority is not protected by sovereign immunity and that the lower courts applied an incorrect legal framework.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues it is protected by sovereign immunity as an instrumentality of the State, a municipal corporation, or an instrumentality of a municipality.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded the case for further consideration of the housing authority's immunity under the proper analytical approach, which involves examining common law.

title: Bailey v. McKintosh County, Webster v. McIntosh County, McIntosh County v. Webster
description: Whether a zoning ordinance passed by McIntosh County, which increased the allowable maximum dwelling size in a historic district, is subject to a citizen-initiated referendum under the Georgia Constitution's Home Rule Provision, with the plaintiff arguing it is not subject to such a referendum and the defendant arguing it is.
plaintiff_argument: McIntosh County argued that its zoning ordinance was passed under the Zoning Provision of the Georgia Constitution, not the Home Rule Provision, and therefore is not subject to the referendum process.
defendant_argument: The Intervenors and Judge Webster argued that the superior court erred in concluding that the zoning ordinance was not subject to the referendum procedures of the Home Rule Provision, asserting that the Home Rule Provision does apply to zoning ordinances.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the superior court's order that halted the referendum and issued a writ of prohibition against Judge Webster, concluding that the zoning ordinance is subject to the Home Rule Provision's referendum procedures. The Court affirmed the superior court's injunction preventing enforcement of the Ordinance pending appeal.

title: Stephens v. State
description: Whether the Georgia statute prohibiting 18- to 20-year-olds from carrying handguns in public violates Article I, Section I, Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Thomas Stephens argued that OCGA § 16-11-126 (g)(1) violates the Georgia Constitution's right to bear arms by prohibiting 18-20 year olds from obtaining weapons licenses and carrying handguns in public, asking the court to overrule its long-standing precedent and apply federal constitutional tests.
defendant_argument: The State contended that the statutory scheme is a reasonable safety measure, not arbitrary, and not a complete prohibition on the right to keep and bear arms, thus a permissible exercise of the police power authorized by the "manner clause" of Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's dismissal, ruling that Stephens failed to provide a compelling argument to reconsider the court's consistent construction of Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution, thereby upholding the statute.

title: State v. Dias
description: Whether evidence of a defendant's refusal to submit to a warrantless blood test is admissible at trial, with the State arguing for its admissibility and Dias arguing against it based on constitutional rights.
plaintiff_argument: The State argues that admitting blood-test refusal evidence does not violate the Fourth or Fifth Amendments or the Georgia Constitution's self-incrimination and search/seizure provisions.
defendant_argument: Dias argues that refusing a warrantless blood test is an exercise of Fourth and Fifth Amendment rights (and Georgia constitutional equivalents) against unlawful search and self-incrimination, and this refusal evidence should not be used against her.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the trial court's judgment that excluded the blood-test refusal evidence and remanded the case for consideration of other non-constitutional grounds for exclusion.

title: Republican National Committee v. Eternal Vigilance Action, Inc; Georgia v. Eternal Vigilance Action
description: Whether the Georgia General Assembly can delegate broad rulemaking authority over elections to the State Elections Board (SEB) without sufficient guidelines, and whether various plaintiffs have standing to challenge these rules.
plaintiff_argument: The SEB rules are unconstitutional and unauthorized by the Election Code, violating the nondelegation doctrine and infringing on the fundamental right to vote, and the plaintiffs have standing to challenge them based on organizational, associational, community-stakeholder, or individual voter rights.
defendant_argument: The SEB rules are constitutional and authorized by the General Assembly with sufficient guidelines, the plaintiffs lack standing to challenge them, and their claims are too vague for declaratory relief.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, reversed in part, and vacated and remanded in part. It ruled that organizational plaintiffs lacked standing, but individual plaintiffs had standing to challenge five of the seven rules. Four of these five rules (Reasonable Inquiry, Examination, Hand Count, Drop Box ID) were found invalid due to unauthorized delegation of legislative power, while the Drop Box Surveillance Rule was upheld. The trial court's finding on Hall's standing as an election board member was vacated and remanded for further consideration. The trial court's finding that SEB rules violated the Federal Elections Clause was reversed.

title: Atlantic Games, Inc. v. Georgia Lottery Corporation
description: Whether the General Assembly's delegation of rulemaking authority to the Georgia Lottery Corporation violated the nondelegation doctrine due to a lack of clear statutory guidance.
plaintiff_argument: Atlantic Games argues that the General Assembly's delegation of rulemaking authority to the Georgia Lottery Corporation lacked clear statutory guidance, violating the Georgia nondelegation doctrine, and asked the court to reconsider a previous decision.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that the delegation of rulemaking authority was permissible and did not violate the nondelegation doctrine.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court denied the petition for certiorari in this case, allowing the lower court's decision to stand.

title: White v. City of Mableton
description: Whether House Bill 839, which incorporates the City of Mableton and creates community improvement districts within it, violates Georgia's Single Subject Rule and precedent by addressing more than one subject matter.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that HB 839 is unconstitutional because it creates "more than one unit of government" (Mableton and CIDs) in a single legislative act, violating the Single Subject Rule and Rea precedent.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argued that HB 839 is constitutional because the creation of Community Improvement Districts (CIDs) is germane and logically connected to the incorporation of Mableton, thus adhering to the Single Subject Rule.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the Appellants' complaint, concluding that HB 839 does not violate the Single Subject Rule or run afoul of Rea.

title: Wasserman v. Franklin County
description: Whether the federal doctrine of third-party standing, which allows a plaintiff to assert the rights of a third party, survives as a means of obtaining standing in Georgia courts.
plaintiff_argument: Wasserman argued that the federal doctrine of third-party standing should be recognized in Georgia courts, allowing her to assert Pham's equal protection rights, or that Georgia's standing rules are preempted, or that Pham assigned his rights to her.
defendant_argument: Franklin County contended that Wasserman lacked standing to assert Pham's equal protection rights under Georgia law, and that the federal third-party standing doctrine should not apply.
decision_outcome: The Georgia Supreme Court overruled its prior precedent that adopted the federal doctrine of third-party standing, concluding it is not compatible with Georgia's constitutional standing rules, and vacated the lower court's judgment, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: Sumrall v. State
description: Whether OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) unconstitutionally restricts access to the courts and the right to prosecute and defend one's cause, and whether the trial court erred in dismissing Sumrall's petition for retroactive first-offender treatment due to lack of prosecuting attorney consent.
plaintiff_argument: Sumrall argued that OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) is unconstitutional as it restricts his access to the courts and right to prosecute and defend his cause, and that the prosecuting attorney's inaction constituted implied consent to his petition.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the statute is constitutional, Sumrall failed to obtain the required prosecutorial consent, and therefore the trial court properly dismissed his petition without a hearing.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's dismissal of Sumrall's petition for retroactive first-offender treatment and the denial of his motion to declare OCGA § 42-8-66 (a) (1) unconstitutional.

title: Hollis v. City of LaGrange
description: Whether the trial court has the authority to review claims that municipal utility charges constitute an illegal tax, with plaintiffs arguing the court has such authority and the City arguing it does not due to constitutional restrictions on legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the City's excessive utility charges were illegal taxes not authorized by the Georgia Constitution or law, and the trial court erred in concluding it lacked authority to review their legal claims.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the Georgia Constitution's Paragraph V (d) prohibits the General Assembly from regulating or fixing public utility charges, and by extension, the judicial branch also lacks the authority to review or regulate these charges.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the trial court's judgment, ruling that the trial court erred in determining it lacked authority to review the plaintiffs' claims, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Gonzalez v. Miller
description: Whether the Open Records Act (ORA) applies to district attorneys' offices, whether a citizen has standing to enforce ORA requests made through counsel, and whether prosecutorial immunity bars official-capacity claims against a district attorney under the ORA.
plaintiff_argument: Miller argued that the District Attorney's office is subject to the ORA, that he has constitutional standing to bring an enforcement action, and that prosecutorial immunity does not bar his claims.
defendant_argument: Gonzalez contended that neither she nor her office is subject to the ORA because district attorneys are constitutional officers of the judicial branch, that she is shielded by prosecutorial immunity, and that Miller lacks constitutional standing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's order, holding that the Open Records Act applies to district attorneys' offices, that Miller has standing to bring the enforcement action, and that prosecutorial immunity does not bar official-capacity claims against the District Attorney.

title: Satcher v. Columbia County
description: Whether the permanent injunction granted to property owners against Columbia County for maintaining a defective stormwater drainage system was barred by the County's sovereign immunity, and whether property owners could recover damages for harms incurred after sending a notice to the county.
plaintiff_argument: The property owners argued that they were entitled to a permanent injunction against the County for a continuing nuisance causing property damage and to recover all damages, including those incurred after providing notice to the County.
defendant_argument: Columbia County argued that sovereign immunity barred the permanent injunction and that the property owners could not recover damages incurred after the notice, citing statute of limitations and proper damage measurement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court vacated the Court of Appeals' opinion upholding the permanent injunction, finding it exceeded the sovereign immunity waiver, and remanded for a new injunction within constitutional limits. The Court also denied the property owners' petition for certiorari regarding damages incurred after notice, deeming it improvidently granted and not presenting a general rule of law.

title: Williams v. Powell
description: Whether OCGA § 16-11-34.1, which criminalizes conduct disrupting legislative meetings, is unconstitutionally overbroad or vague under the Georgia Constitution, thereby infringing on free speech rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that OCGA § 16-11-34.1 (a), (f), and (g) are unconstitutionally overbroad and vague, similar to a previously invalidated statute, and that its terms fail to provide clear notice or guidance, thus violating free speech protections. They also argued that State Representative Park Cannon's specific actions were protected speech and not disruptive.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that OCGA § 16-11-34.1 is not unconstitutionally overbroad or vague, as it is more narrowly tailored than the previously invalidated statute, and that Cannon's as-applied claim failed because her alleged conduct was not prohibited by the statute.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's dismissal of the appellants' facial challenges to OCGA § 16-11-34.1 as unconstitutionally overbroad or vague, and also affirmed the dismissal of State Representative Park Cannon's as-applied challenge.

title: Cobb County v. Floam
description: Whether the Floams were entitled to declaratory relief regarding the constitutionality of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners' amendment changing commission district boundaries, with the Floams arguing they faced uncertainty warranting such relief and Cobb County arguing they did not.
plaintiff_argument: The Floams argued that the Cobb County Board of Commissioners' amendment changing district boundaries was unconstitutional, and they sought a declaratory judgment because they faced uncertainty regarding their voting rights and district representation, which constituted an individualized injury.
defendant_argument: Cobb County argued that the Floams lacked constitutional standing because they did not allege an individualized injury, and even if they had standing, they did not demonstrate the requisite uncertainty about future decisions to warrant declaratory relief.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the trial court's decision, concluding that while the Floams had constitutional standing as community stakeholders, they did not show the necessary uncertainty about their future conduct to obtain declaratory relief, and therefore their claim must be dismissed without reaching the merits of the constitutional arguments.

title: Lovell v. Raffensperger
description: Whether actions seeking declaratory relief from acts of the state or local government, relying on Paragraph V's waiver of sovereign immunity, must be brought exclusively against the state or local government in their official name, or if naming individual officers or entities is sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that their complaints, which named the Secretary of State and local board members, complied with Paragraph V's waiver of sovereign immunity, and thus the dismissals were erroneous.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs' complaints failed to comply with Paragraph V's requirements for waiving sovereign immunity, specifically by not exclusively naming the State of Georgia or the relevant local government.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial courts' dismissal of the actions, concluding that the appellants failed to comply with Paragraph V (b) (2) by not exclusively naming the State of Georgia or the relevant local government as defendants.

title: In Re: Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission Rules and Code of Conduct
description: Whether the Supreme Court of Georgia has the constitutional power to adopt the draft standards of conduct and rules for the Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission.
plaintiff_argument: The Prosecuting Attorneys Qualifications Commission transmitted draft standards and rules for the Court's review and adoption, implicitly seeking the Court's approval and suggesting it has the power to do so.
defendant_argument: The Supreme Court expressed grave doubts about its constitutional power to adopt the standards and rules, citing separation of powers and the nature of judicial versus executive power exercised by district attorneys.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court respectfully declined to take any action regarding the Commission's draft standards of conduct and rules for its governance.

title: Roberts v. Cuthpert
description: Whether the General Assembly waived sovereign immunity and whether judicial immunity was waived for a claim of costs and attorney's fees against a probate judge for denying a weapons carry license, and whether such recovery violates the Separation of Powers Provision of the Georgia Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Roberts argued that the General Assembly waived sovereign immunity and the probate judge waived judicial immunity for the costs-and-fees claim, and that recovering such fees does not violate the Separation of Powers Provision because denying a weapons carry license is not a judicial function.
defendant_argument: The probate judges argued that sovereign immunity and judicial immunity barred Roberts's claims for costs and attorney's fees, and that the recovery of such fees was unconstitutional under the Separation of Powers Provision as it infringes on judicial independence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part the superior court's judgment, ruling that sovereign immunity was waived, judicial immunity was waived by the probate judge for the costs-and-fees claim in his official capacity, and the recovery of costs and attorney's fees does not violate the Separation of Powers Provision, remanding the case for a hearing on costs.

title: Raffensperger v. Jackson
description: Whether the Georgia Lactation Consultant Practice Act, which restricts who can provide lactation care for compensation, violates the due process rights of individuals to pursue their chosen profession.
plaintiff_argument: The Act is unconstitutional, irrational, and violates their due process and equal protection rights by preventing them from practicing their lawful profession as lactation care providers.
defendant_argument: The Act does not prevent plaintiffs from pursuing their profession and is rationally related to protecting public health, safety, and welfare by promoting access to quality care.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the trial court's ruling, concluding that the Georgia Lactation Consultant Practice Act is unconstitutional as it violates the plaintiffs' due process rights.

title: In re Judge Christian Coomer
description: Whether the Judicial Qualifications Commission (JQC) has jurisdiction over a judge's conduct that occurred before they became a judge or judicial candidate, and whether negligent conduct outside a judicial capacity can warrant discipline.
plaintiff_argument: The JQC Director argued that the JQC has jurisdiction over conduct occurring before a person became a judge or judicial candidate, and that even mere negligence for actions taken outside a judicial capacity could warrant discipline.
defendant_argument: Judge Coomer argued that the JQC lacked jurisdiction over pre-judicial conduct because the Code of Judicial Conduct does not apply to such actions, and that disciplining him for such conduct would violate due process rights. He also contended that the JQC's authority over judicial candidates is limited to campaigning and politics.
decision_outcome: The court remanded the case to the JQC Hearing Panel, ruling that the Code of Judicial Conduct does not apply to pre-judicial conduct and that discipline for non-judicial conduct requires a finding of bad faith, not mere negligence.

title: Session v. State
description: Whether Derrick Session's convictions for failure to register as a sex offender in Georgia should be overturned due to insufficient evidence, violations of his federal rights to travel and equal protection, or a violation of the Georgia constitutional prohibition against legislation regarding the social status of citizens.
plaintiff_argument: Session argued that the evidence was insufficient, the Georgia registration statute violated his federal rights to travel and equal protection by treating him worse than a native Georgian, and the statute facially violated the Georgia constitutional prohibition against legislation regarding the social status of citizens.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the evidence was sufficient, Session's federal rights arguments were based on speculative assumptions, and he failed to show the Georgia registration statute violated the social status provision.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Session's convictions for failure to register as a sex offender, rejecting all his arguments.

title: Johnson v. State
description: Whether a pro se filing made by a defendant who is actually or presumptively represented by counsel is always a legal nullity.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that such pro se filings should not always be considered legal nullities, as courts should have discretion to recognize them, especially when counsel fails to act to preserve appeal rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant implicitly argues that such pro se filings should be considered legal nullities, based on past precedent that treated them as "invalid" or "unauthorized and without effect."
decision_outcome: The court overruled past decisions that held pro se filings by counseled defendants are always legal nullities, affirming that courts retain discretion to allow hybrid representation, and vacated the lower court's judgment, remanding the case for reconsideration of Johnson's pro se filings.

title: Taylor v. The Devereux Foundation
description: Whether the statutory cap on punitive damages in OCGA § 51-12-5.1 (g) violates the Georgia Constitution's right to trial by jury, separation of powers, and equal protection.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (Taylor) argued that the punitive damages cap violates the Georgia Constitution's right to trial by jury, separation of powers, and equal protection.
defendant_argument: The defendant (Devereux) argued that the punitive damages cap does not violate the Georgia Constitution and that Taylor failed to prove otherwise.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, ruling that the punitive damages cap in OCGA § 51-12-5.1 (g) does not violate the Georgia Constitution and upheld the reduction of the punitive damages award to $250,000.

title: State v. SASS Group
description: Whether the term "action" in Paragraph V of the Georgia Constitution, which waives sovereign immunity for certain suits against the State, refers to an entire lawsuit or only a specific claim within a lawsuit, thereby determining if a suit naming additional defendants must be dismissed in its entirety.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that "action" means a claim or cause of action, not an entire lawsuit, allowing them to include claims against the State (under Paragraph V's waiver) and other defendants in the same lawsuit, with only the Paragraph V-reliant claims needing to comply with exclusivity.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that "action" means the entire case or lawsuit, and therefore, if any claim in a lawsuit relies on Paragraph V's waiver, the entire suit must be brought exclusively against the State or be dismissed.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the State's motion to dismiss, vacated the interlocutory injunction, and remanded the case with direction that it be dismissed.

title: Camden County v. Sweatt
description: Whether the Home Rule Paragraph of the Georgia Constitution authorizes county electorates to petition for a special election to repeal resolutions adopted by the county's governing authority, with the County arguing it does not and the electors arguing it does.
plaintiff_argument: Camden County argued that the Home Rule Paragraph does not authorize referendums on resolutions adopted by the county's governing authority, limiting such referendums to 'local acts' only.
defendant_argument: Sweatt, et al. (the electors) argued that the Home Rule Paragraph explicitly grants the electorate the power to seek a referendum on the amendment or repeal of 'ordinances, resolutions, or regulations adopted pursuant to subparagraph (a).'
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the superior court's denial of Camden County's petition for declaratory relief, mandamus, and prohibition, thereby upholding the validity of the referendum.

title: Ammons v. State
description: Whether evidence of a defendant's refusal to perform preliminary breath tests and field sobriety tests violates the Georgia Constitution's right against compelled self-incrimination, and whether statutes allowing evidence of refusal to consent to a blood test violate the Georgia Privileges and Immunities Clause.
plaintiff_argument: Ammons argued that using evidence of her refusal to perform breath and field sobriety tests violates her right against self-incrimination, and that statutes permitting evidence of her refusal to consent to a blood test violate the General Assembly's constitutional duty to protect citizens' rights, privileges, and immunities.
defendant_argument: The State argued that evidence of Ammons's refusal to perform tests is admissible and does not violate the Georgia Constitution, relying on prior precedent for preliminary breath tests and asserting that the Privileges and Immunities Clause does not bar admission of blood test refusal evidence.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and reversed in part, ruling that evidence of refusal to perform preliminary breath and field sobriety tests is inadmissible, but evidence of refusal to consent to a blood test is admissible.

title: Reed v. State
description: Whether Jaquavious Reed's conviction for murder and other charges should be overturned due to alleged errors including insufficient evidence, appellate delay, denial of right to be present, prosecutorial conflict, incomplete transcript, Brady violation, denial of continuance, ineffective assistance of counsel, and improper sentencing.
plaintiff_argument: Reed argued his conviction should be overturned due to insufficient evidence, inordinate appellate delay, denial of his right to be present at bench conferences, a conflict of interest with the DA's office, an incomplete trial transcript, a Brady violation, denial of a continuance for a surprise witness, ineffective assistance of counsel, and improper sentencing.
defendant_argument: The State argued the evidence was sufficient, Reed failed to show prejudice from appellate delay or incomplete transcript, his right to be present was not violated or was waived, the conflict of interest claim was waived, there was no Brady violation, and the denial of continuance was not an abuse of discretion, while conceding the improper sentencing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed Reed's conviction for malice murder, vacated his conviction for felony murder, and remanded the case for resentencing, denying all other claims for overturning the conviction.

title: Prickett v. State
description: Whether Prickett's conviction for felony murder and other charges should be overturned due to ineffective assistance of counsel, violation of his constitutional right to be present at critical trial stages, and the trial court's failure to address prosecutorial misconduct.
plaintiff_argument: Prickett argued that his trial counsel was ineffective for failing to stipulate his felon status, his constitutional right to be present was violated by unrecorded bench conferences, and the trial court erred by not rebuking the prosecutor or declaring a mistrial after an improper closing argument.
defendant_argument: The State implicitly argued that trial counsel's performance was not deficient or did not cause prejudice, that Prickett's presence was not required at the bench conferences or he acquiesced to his counsel's waiver, and that any prosecutorial error was harmless given the strong evidence of guilt and jury instructions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed Prickett's convictions but vacated his sentences and remanded the case for resentencing due to errors in the sentencing order.

title: Awad v. State
description: Whether Paragraph XVI of the Georgia Constitution prohibits the State from admitting into evidence a defendant's refusal to submit to a state-administered urine test for chemical testing, on the grounds that it violates the right against compelled self-incrimination.
plaintiff_argument: Awad argued that the right against compelled self-incrimination protected by Paragraph XVI of the Georgia Constitution prohibits the State from admitting evidence of his refusal to submit to a urine test, as providing a urine sample in a collection container requires an affirmative act that generates self-incriminating evidence.
defendant_argument: The State argued that obtaining a urine sample does not implicate the right against compelled self-incrimination because it does not require an 'act' on the part of the defendant, comparing it to other bodily substances like DNA or blood, and that commenting on refusal does not necessarily implicate rights under Paragraph XVI.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals' decision, holding that the trial court properly suppressed evidence of Awad's refusal to submit to a urine test, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Harvey v. Merchan
description: Whether OCGA § 9-3-33.1, which revives time-barred civil claims for childhood sexual abuse, can apply to acts that occurred outside Georgia and whether its retroactive application violates Georgia's constitutional ban on retroactive laws or federal and state due process and equal protection clauses.
plaintiff_argument: Merchan argued that Georgia substantive law and its statute of limitations should apply to all claims, including those from Quebec, under a "continuing tort" theory, and that OCGA § 9-3-33.1 is constitutional and applies to out-of-state acts.
defendant_argument: The Harveys argued Merchan's claims were time-barred, could not be revived by OCGA § 9-3-33.1 because it doesn't apply to out-of-state acts or acts after age 18, and that the revival provision violates constitutional prohibitions against retroactive laws, due process, and equal protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part and vacated in part, remanding the case for the trial court to compare the respective limitations periods, concluding that the revival statute applies to out-of-state acts and is constitutional.

title: Duke v. State
description: Whether an indigent defendant represented by private, pro bono counsel has a statutory or constitutional right to state-funded experts and investigators needed to prepare a defense, with the plaintiff arguing they do and the defendant arguing they do not.
plaintiff_argument: Duke argued that as an indigent defendant, he is entitled to state-funded ancillary defense services under the Indigent Defense Act (IDA), and his choice of pro bono counsel should not impede this right to due process and a fair trial.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Duke was no longer indigent under the IDA due to his pro bono counsel, that the IDA provides no mechanism for state funding for ancillary services in such cases, and that Duke waived his right to state-funded services by choosing private counsel.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's ruling that pro bono counsel qualifies as 'other resources' and that the Indigent Defense Act provides no mechanism for indigent defendants with pro bono counsel to obtain state-funded ancillary defense services, and remanded the case for further proceedings.
